Aaron Vale lies in the dark listening to a heart that was not his an hour ago. The breathing comes without effort. He cannot stop thinking about whose it was.

A mathematician who has been short of breath on staircases sits in a cardiology clinic. The doctor shows him numbers. The muscle is finished. Weeks, not months. The only thing that helps is somebody else dying at the right time.

His wife, who has been out of the house for a year, sits across the kitchen table with a clinic form. She asks him to sign while he still can. What is in the freezer is all there will ever be. He tells her he is not coming back and that he does not want the child. She says the thing that is true: he is spending a life somebody else paid for.

A woman who used to be somebody else does the school run, keeps the garden, has not had anything in her system for years. Two girls and a husband who adores her, in a house with a fixed rate on it. She is taken into a side room off a corridor and told about her husband, and then, while she is still on the first thing, about both children. She starts again the way somebody starts a job, in the bathroom of a bar with the door locked, and then in the house, and then at the kitchen table with the girls' drawings still on the wall behind her.

An ex-convict with scripture inked up both forearms holds down a job, runs a boys' team on Saturdays, testifies to anyone who will sit still. His wife watches the certainty in him the way you watch weather coming. The faith and the temper are the same thing wearing different clothes. A pickup comes through a crossing at the wrong moment and takes a man and two children off their feet. It goes on a hundred yards, stops, sits there with the engine running, backs up a little, and then goes. He walks up the steps of a police station on his own, waits at the counter, tells the desk sergeant what he did at the crossing and how far he drove afterwards. He is back inside within the month. Released early on somebody's recommendation, he gets as far as the gate, looks at the family waiting for him, and keeps walking. He takes a job cleaning rooms at a motel four hundred miles from any of it.

Aaron pays a man in a car park to find out whose heart he is carrying. It is against every rule there is. He pays him anyway, and is handed a name and a street. He follows the woman for a week, learns which pool she swims at, arranges to be in the water at the same hour until it stops being a coincidence. Within a fortnight he is in her house. He says it in her kitchen, badly: what is beating in his chest belonged to her husband. She puts him out of the house that night with everything he brought. Four days later she asks him to come back, and he does.

She says she cannot go on breathing in the same country as the man who drove away from the crossing. She keeps saying it until it is the only thing in the house. He buys a pistol from a man in a lock-up and drives out to the motel with it under the seat. He gets the other man against a wall in the dark behind the building and cannot make his hand do it. The shot goes somewhere it will not kill. He stands over him telling him to get up and run. The wounded man follows the two of them back to their own room, bleeding through his shirt, stands in the doorway asking to be finished. The gun turns round and goes into the other chest instead.

They get him into a car and drive with the horn down. The borrowed heart stops on the table anyway. The man who drove away from the crossing goes back to the family he walked out on. The woman goes home on her own, carrying something.

Eight men in black suits sat round a diner table pulling apart what a pop song was really about and whether a woman who brings coffee has earned anything extra for it. Nobody used a real name. The one called Mr. Elm stirred his eggs and listened the way a man listens when he is counting exits.

Three weeks earlier, in a police safe room with no windows, a handler named Pruitt had sat across from Danny Roarke and made him tell the same story forty times. A bag of drugs in a public lavatory. Four dogs. A collar that went wrong. Pruitt stopped him each time, corrected a gesture, a pause, a word, until Danny stopped reciting it and started remembering it. The story had to be lived in, not learned. Then Danny walked into a bar and told it to a room of men who had heard every kind of liar, got the laugh in the right place, and walked out with a job and a colour-free name he did not pick. The boss Bram nodded. His son Cal watched. Mr. Ash poured him a drink.

Back at the office Bram dealt out tree names off a list so that no man in the room could give up another. Mr. Birch spent a minute arguing that his was the worst of them. Nobody laughed.

The robbery collapsed inside a minute. The alarm was already running when they came out, and Mr. Ash fired through the windscreen and out of both side windows while the car went down the wrong street. Fleeing on foot, Mr. Elm dragged a woman out of her own car, and she had a pistol in the door pocket and put one into his stomach before he could get the door shut. He shot her and drove away bleeding.

Mr. Ash reached the warehouse with the man screaming in the back. He carried him in, laid him down on the ramp in the blood he was already losing, held his head and told him nobody dies here today. Elm could not answer.

Years before any of this, a man named Ren Vasco had walked out of prison and straight into Bram's office. He could have shortened that sentence by talking. He did not. Bram handed him an envelope and a place on the job by way of thanks, and Cal understood that the debt was now being paid in work.

Mr. Birch arrived at the warehouse clean and furious. He walked the room through the timings and said the police were on the pavement before the first alarm. One of the men in this room had called it in. Then he went outside and put the diamonds somewhere nobody watching him could see.

Ren strolled in late and unhurried, complained about the shouting, and opened the boot of his car. He dragged out a young patrolman named Doyle, hands bound behind him, and dropped him on a chair.

Left alone with the bound officer, Ren found a station playing something from twenty years ago, turned it up, danced a few steps, took the man's ear off with a razor and talked into it. Then he emptied a can of petrol over him. Doyle learned that nobody was coming.

From the floor, with nothing left, the dying man emptied his gun into the one holding the lighter. Ren dropped. Mr. Elm told Doyle that he was a police officer, and that there were cars in the street outside waiting for Bram to arrive.

Cal returned to a body and a story. He listened to the version he was given, decided it held, and put three rounds into the officer on the chair himself to close the matter.

Bram walked in. He looked at the man on the floor for a long moment and said flatly that this was the one. The informer. The man who had carried him in put his gun on the boss instead and would not be told otherwise.

Three guns came up at once in a room the size of a garage and all three went off. When it stopped, Bram and Cal were silent. Ash and Elm were still making a noise.

Bleeding out beside him, the officer said it plainly, because the man had earned it. He was a police officer. He had always been a police officer. Ash dragged himself up, put the gun to Elm's head, and the doors came in as he fired and he was cut down where he knelt.

On the morning he turned twenty-five, Emmett Rusk took control of the fortune and told the banker Barrow that of all his holdings he wanted only the failing city newspaper, the Clarion. He thought it might be fun. He moved a bed into the offices, installed his manager Marsh on one side and his friend Devlin on the other, and printed a signed statement of principles on the front page. Then he hired away the entire staff of the rival paper across the street by simply paying them more, and threw a party with a brass band and a chorus line, dancing in the middle of it himself.

He returned from a buying trip abroad engaged to Adele, the governor's niece. The wedding was on every front page but his own. Then a run of breakfasts, further apart each time—the talk shortening, the table lengthening—until they sat at either end reading rival newspapers, one of which he owned.

Splashed by a cab on his way somewhere else, he was laughing at the mud on his coat outside a chemist's when a shopgirl with toothache laughed back. He started visiting Nora Kell's rooms in the evenings and told nobody.

Ten days before the ballot, the party boss Halloran brought Adele up the stairs to Nora's rooms and offered a straight trade: withdraw on grounds of health, or be on every front page by Monday. Emmett told him to get out of the building. He lost the election. The Clarion printed FRAUD AT THE POLLS across six columns. Devlin asked to be transferred. Adele went without either of them raising a voice.

He married Nora. He bought her a teacher, then a house to sing in, on the grounds that people were going to be made to think of her as a singer whether or not she was one. The debut was unbearable. Devlin, brought back to cover it, got drunk and fell asleep over half a savage paragraph. Emmett finished the sentence in the same direction, set it, printed it, and fired him.

Nora was found in a dark hotel room with the glass beside her. When she could speak she said she would rather have died than go out in front of them again. He told her she could stop.

He moved her into the half-finished palace on the hill, Silvermount, where the ceilings were too high to heat and the crates were never unpacked. She did jigsaw puzzles on the floor of a hall the size of a station. After a picnic on a black beach where nobody enjoyed anything, and a quarrel that carried through the canvas, she packed in the morning. He told her she could not go. She went.

He took her room apart with his hands. He stopped at a glass snow globe, murmured one word to nobody—Bluebell—and carried it out past a facing pair of mirrors that gave back an old man repeated until he was too small to see.

He died in a bed at Silvermount with the word on his lips again and let the globe go. It rolled off the boards and broke on the step.

A newsreel obituary recapped his public life—the palace, the papers, the two wives, the politics, the collapse—and closed without explaining his last word. The reporter Nash was sent to find out what it meant. He started with Nora, drunk at a table in a seaside club at four in the afternoon, who told him to get out before he finished the sentence.

Nash read Barrow's memoir in a marble library. The memoir told of a mining boarding house out west, where a lodger who could not pay his board left a worthless deed behind, and the seam under it turned out to be enormous. At the kitchen table Emmett's mother signed the boy and the money over to the banker from the east, the father objecting from the doorway and being ignored. The memoir told of the yard in the snow, where the boy put his sled into the banker's stomach hard enough to sit him down, and was taken east that evening regardless. The sled was painted with a name. Bluebell.

Nash sat with Marsh, with Devlin, with Nora a second time, with the old butler Colm. He put his notebook away. No one word ever explains a life. Below him, workmen clearing the hall of crates put a small sled into the furnace.

Two hitmen in dark suits drove across the city arguing about drug laws abroad and what a hamburger was called there. Neither mentioned the job. In the corridor outside the flat they had come for, they argued about whether a foot massage was worth killing a man for, the guns still in the bag. Then Marcus recited a passage of scripture at a terrified young man named Tobin, and he and Rollo shot him for skimming from the man who employed them. They took the briefcase. A man nobody thought to search for burst from the bathroom and emptied a revolver at them from six feet away. Every round missed. Marcus stood in front of the pattern of holes in the wall behind him and called it divine intervention. In the car afterwards Rollo's gun went off over a bump and took the head off the man in the back seat. The interior was unusable in a second. Marcus pulled the bloodied car into a friend's garage in a quiet suburb, where a soft-spoken man arrived, timed the work to the minute, had them hosed down in the yard and dressed in borrowed shorts and T-shirts. The two carried the briefcase into a near-empty bar dressed like students. At the counter the man who employed them was counting notes into the hand of an ageing boxer and telling him which round to go down in.

Over coffee and eggs in a diner, a couple worked out that liquor stores had got dangerous and nobody ever robs a restaurant. They were up on the booth seats with the pistol out before the plates were cleared. Marcus let the pistol be held on him, handed over his own wallet, recited the passage again and explained what he had decided it meant. He kept the briefcase and let the two of them walk out the door.

Rollo drove out to a dealer's house, paid for a bag of unusually pure heroin, and shot up at the kitchen table before going back to the car. He took his employer's wife to a themed restaurant where waiters played at being stars of an earlier decade, and the two of them took their shoes off and won the dance contest. Back at the flat she found the bag in his coat, took it for cocaine, and snorted a line. She went blue on the carpet and was brought back by a needle of adrenaline driven into her chest on the dealer's living-room floor.

Years earlier, a returning prisoner of war sat a small boy down in a bare front room and put into his hands the gold watch his father had carried through years of captivity and kept hidden to the end. The boy grew into the ageing boxer who did not go down in the fifth. He won, hit the other man hard enough that he never got up, and was out of the arena and into a passing taxi before the crowd understood what it watched. In a motel room on the edge of town he asked his girlfriend whether she had packed the watch. She had not. It was still on the bedside table in a flat that was certainly being watched. He let himself in and found it exactly where it was left. He was at the kitchen counter when a hitman came out of the bathroom, and the submachine gun lying on the counter was nearer to him than the man was to his own. Driving away, he stopped at a light and found the man hunting him crossing the road with a paper bag in his arms. He put the car through him. Both wrecked. Both were dragged down into the basement of a pawnshop by the men who owned it. He got out of his restraints and was at the street door when he stopped, took a sword down off the shop wall, and went back down for the man who was hunting him. Afterwards his employer told him they were square, on the condition that he never came back. He collected his girlfriend from the motel, put her on the back of a motorcycle taken from the pawnshop, and rode out with the watch back on his wrist.

Four adults, a baby and a rottweiler in a house built for two. Ruben slept on the couch and spent most of the day watching his brother's wife move about the kitchen. His mother kept the peace. Nestor kept none. He came home from robbing a chemist's with a scarf still in his pocket and knocked Alma across the kitchen for asking where the money was. After that Ruben started saying she should come away with him, quietly at first and then not quietly.

The dog came back off the street having killed something bigger than itself, and a neighbour explained what that was worth. Within a month Tigre was going into a ring twice a week and coming out of it every time, and Ruben was saving what it earned. He gave two men in a bar the address of his own brother. Nestor came out of hospital, worked out who had arranged it in about a day, and left with Alma, the baby and every note hidden in the wardrobe.

The fights went on. In the last one the promoter Chaco lost too much and put a pistol into the dog's side in the middle of the ring. Ruben went over the rope with a knife into him and was out the door and into the truck with his friend Pipo before anyone moved. The truck came through a red light at sixty with the dog bleeding across the back seat and took the side out of a small car turning across the junction.

Weeks later, Nestor went into a bank with the same scarf and was shot on the floor of it. At the funeral Ruben made the offer one last time, and his brother's widow looked at him and said no and meant it.

---

A married man walked out on a wife and two daughters at a birthday party and moved Celine into a new flat with a floor-to-ceiling window, directly opposite the hoarding carrying her own face. She came round in hospital with a cage of steel pins holding her leg together and asked first about her lapdog Chispa, which had been in the new flat with nobody in it and had not been seen since. The little dog had gone through a gap in the boards and could not get back, and its whining came up through the floor of every room. Hector took the boards up one by one with a crowbar while her leg went bad above him. It came off above the knee in the end. In the same week the hoarding across the road was stripped and pasted over with something else, and the two of them sat in the wrecked flat looking at a blank frame.

---

A vagrant pushing a cart of scrap through the junction stood in the smoke, looked at the two wrecks and the people running towards them, and took the bleeding dog out of the back seat and walked away with it. Cardo got Tigre back on his feet over weeks in a yard full of strays, feeding it by hand. It slept against him and followed him out into the street in the morning.

A man in a good suit met him behind a church, handed him a photograph of his own half-brother and business partner, and named a figure. Cardo took half in advance and asked no questions. He stood a long way back at his own wife's burial among people who thought he had died twenty years ago, and then walked behind his grown daughter Perla through three streets and stopped outside her building.

A wife who tested him to death. A claim denied. The voice listened and said nothing until Martin was done.

A year before, a plainclothes officer named Roy had walked Martin through the evidence to a derelict building out past the edge of town. Roy stood by while Martin shot the second intruder, the one who had gotten out of the house. Within minutes Martin was asking who they were looking for. Roy told him. Martin forgot. It was finished, and it was never finished.

The voice on the telephone gave him a name, a trade, and an address. Gil Marsh, dealer. The man would be in a basement on the east side. Martin wrote it all down as fact and pocketed the note.

Out in a field somewhere between then and now, Martin fed a hairbrush and a paperback into a small fire. They were his wife's things. He waited for something to end inside him, but the loss would not stay long enough to grieve. The fire went down. He walked away not certain what he had been doing.

In the basement Martin beat a man half his weight, got a belt round his throat, and held it. Then he took the picture. The Polaroid developed in his hand and he wrote the date and the name across the bottom in block capitals.

Before any of this, in a rented room, Martin had turned himself into a filing cabinet. Instant photographs captioned in capitals, notes clipped to notes, and the facts he trusted most cut into his own skin where he could not lose them. He trusted his handwriting over his head.

The dying man said one word. Elias. It meant nothing to Martin, who could not ask again. He changed into the dead man's suit, took the keys, and drove the sports car away into a life that was not his.

Two men had come through the bathroom door at night. Martin shot one across his wife's body. The other put him into the mirror head first. From that moment nothing new would stay. His wife was dead. A second man had gotten out. He would hunt him with notes and ink and photographs until the notes told him to stop.

Roy sat Martin down in the derelict building and laid it out. The dealer was nobody. The revenge was taken a year ago. The case Martin recited to strangers on the telephone was not a case at all but his own house, his own wife, his own condition. Martin was Elias Prine.

In a suburban living room a woman had put her watch forward and asked her husband for her injection. Then she asked again, and again. He gave her each one as though it were the first. She died believing the condition was real. She was right.

Rather than hold a truth that would leave him nothing, Martin burned the photographs of Gil Marsh. He wrote three words across Roy's picture—HE IS LYING—and copied the registration off the car outside as the next thing he would be certain of.

Working a claim from behind a desk, Martin Kray had put a soft-spoken man through test after test and written the memory loss down as something the mind was doing to itself. The insurer paid nothing. Elias Prine walked out with no care and no witness to what he was.

Martin walked into a tattoo parlour with the note in his fist and had the registration inked down his thigh under the five facts already there. He did not remember writing the note. The lie was now permanent.

At a bar he did not know he had been to before, a woman behind the counter watched a stranger come in wearing a suit she recognized, parking a car she recognized outside. Corinne smiled, took his order, and had the staff do something to the beer before it reached him.

She cleared every pen out of her house first. Then she said the things that would make him swing, waited outside until the bruises came up, and came back in blaming a man called Vance. Martin wrote the name down as fact.

He waited in the dark of another motel bathroom, took Vance down as he came through, and drove him out of town with a gun in his ribs and a warning he would not himself remember giving.

Corinne had a friend at the registry run the plate off the note he left lying about. She put the printout into his hand across the table. Roy Mercer. The false fact now had a face.

Martin brought the officer out to the same derelict building on a pretext, walked him into the room, and put one through his head. He photographed what was left, satisfied that the note was right. The note was his own handwriting, and it was a lie, and he would never know.

For six months he had not slept. Then by accident he sat in a church hall full of dying people and one of them held him, and that night he went under like a stone. He went back four evenings a week. He wept at diseases he did not have and slept the sleep of the genuinely ill.

He was standing in a stairwell in a tower he did not yet know existed, and the gun in the other man's hand was in his own. He put it in his mouth, angled it toward the back of his teeth, and fired through his cheek.

He came back to the folding chairs. A woman started appearing in the same circles, smoking through the meditation, her performance so thin he could see daylight through it. The moment he could see the lie in her he could see it in himself, and the sleep stopped. Her name was Ada Vey.

She was brought to a high window by shaven men who apologised and left. The two of them stood holding hands, his face wrapped in gauze, and outside the buildings went down one after another in order.

On a night flight he sat next to a soap salesman named Rex Marrow who talked for forty minutes about how everything either of them owned had been chosen for them by someone else. He pocketed the card. He came home from a trip to find his windows on the pavement and every catalogue item gone. He did not ring the woman. He rang the salesman, who took him to a derelict house at the edge of the industrial district with no working plumbing.

Rex held his wet hand flat on the kitchen table and tipped lye onto the back of it. He would not let him retreat into the cave or count breaths. He made him stay in the minute. The scar would still be there at the end.

Outside a bar Rex handed him a beer and asked, quite seriously, to be hit as hard as he could. They went at each other on the tarmac until neither could stand and both were laughing. Two men in a car park became a weekly thing in a cellar with rules read aloud at the start, and then the cellar was full, and then there was a waiting list.

In a motel room with flight records and receipts spread over the bed, it went together: one body, one bank account, one man awake and asleep, every conversation between the two of them held in an empty room. There was no other man and there never was.

Ada overdosed. Rex brought her back to the derelict house, and for weeks the two of them were audible through every floor while he lay rigid downstairs. Rex rendered fat stolen from a cosmetic surgery clinic into soap on the kitchen stove and sold it back to the department stores at eighty dollars a bar. Rex burned his hand with lye and held him there. He walked into his employer's office, said what he wanted, and when he was refused he beat his own face into the carpet and let security find them. He was paid to stay away.

He got her on the telephone and asked her, badly, whose bed she had been in. She said his, obviously, and asked what was wrong with him. The last thing he was holding on to went.

The cellar became a name and a doctrine. Havoc. The house filled with shaven recruits who slept on the floor and went out at night to break corporate property. Rex took both hands off the wheel on a wet road, asked the men in the back what they wished they had done, and let the car go into the oncoming lane. When the narrator came round in the ditch, Rex was not there and was not anywhere. A member named Ogden was shot dead coming out of a job with a drill in his hand, and the house recited his name all night, and the narrator started trying to shut the thing down.

He flew city to city and found the same cellar under every bar, the same rules on the same wall. Barmen looked up, recognised him, and used the other man's name. He worked out what the target had been all along: vans in the car parks beneath the towers that held every record of who owed what, wired and timed and waiting.

Rex took him down a service stairwell a flight at a time. At the bottom he understood that the gun was in his own hand. He put it in his mouth and fired through his cheek to kill Rex, and the other man was gone.

Ada was delivered to the tower by the shaven recruits, who apologised and left. The two of them stood at the window holding hands, his face wrapped, and outside the buildings came down one after another in order.

In a northern port, Solly Two Coats and his crew dressed as devout pilgrims to cross the guarded showroom of a diamond house. They dropped their disguises only at the exit and walked out with one exceptional stone. Before Solly could even admire it, his cousin Marv called from overseas with a terse instruction: bring the stone straight over. The theft had become a delivery job.

Grigor the Nail, meanwhile, told Solly about a bookmaker's in the city where he could place a wager on the fights. Simultaneously, Grigor tipped off the pawnbrokers Ike and Benno to rob Solly there. Neither side understood the collision Grigor had arranged.

Across town, the boxing promoters Halloway and Digby sent their fighter Pretty Sam to buy a caravan from a camp of travellers. Sam treated the residents with contempt, and a quarrel erupted over the deal. The bare-knuckle fighter Finn knocked Sam out cold, leaving the promoters without a man for the gang boss Coldstone's fixed bout. Halloway had no choice but to put Finn in the fight. He stood in Coldstone's office and promised the boss that Finn would go down in the fourth round.

Solly landed in the city, delivered the stone to the fence Hersch for safekeeping, and headed for the bookmaker's carrying a case that no longer held the diamond. He was a visible target now, carrying nothing of value. Ike, Benno, and Tulley burst in to rob the bookmaker's. They seized Solly's arm and his case amid alarms and confusion, then fled—chased off by Grigor himself, the very man who had arranged their job.

That same night, Finn stepped into the ring. Instead of waiting for the agreed round, he ended the contest with one blow in the first. Coldstone lost a fortune and took it out on Halloway.

Marv flew in, found Solly gone, and hired the bounty hunter Ledge to find him. Ledge's method was simple: follow the least competent people in the chain.

Grigor took Solly to an underworld workshop, cut off his arm to get the case open, and found it empty. The stone had been removed before the robbery. Brutality had produced only a hollow container.

Ledge traced the pawnbrokers, shot their car to pieces in the street, and took both them and the stone they had since retrieved from Hersch. The diamond and its vulnerable captives were now travelling together.

Coldstone disposed of the mutilated Solly by feeding him to his pigs. He made Halloway and Digby watch, and told them what would happen to them if the second fight went wrong. The promoters told Finn to go down in the fourth. Then Coldstone's men went to the travellers' camp and burned Finn's mother to death in her caravan. Coercion had become a blood debt.

Grigor ambushed Ledge's car with Ike and Benno inside. The shootout killed Ledge, Grigor, and Benno. Tulley got away with a dog that had swallowed the diamond, hidden better than any safe could manage.

At the rematch, Finn waited until the named fourth round. Then he knocked his opponent out again. Throughout the crowd, armed travellers opened fire on Coldstone's men, massacring them where they sat. Halloway and Digby found Coldstone isolated in the aftermath and shot him. By morning, the travellers had vanished.

The dog was handed in at a pet shop. It coughed up the diamond on the examining table. Halloway and Digby stood over it, the two promoters who had never joined the original theft, holding the prize that had survived every hand it passed through.

The room seemed to rearrange itself around a fact that had been sitting in it undisturbed for years.

He had telephoned Emlyn in a state, earlier that evening. The call came because of what Odile had said in a bar two years after everything was supposed to have ended — that her marriage was over, that she had spent the previous night confessing the whole affair to Emlyn at last. Wilder had believed her. He had carried that belief like a stone in his pocket, the idea that the reckoning was fresh, that the ground had only just given way.

And then Odile had let slip, over her second drink, that Emlyn had been publishing a writer Wilder represented — a novelist both men quietly detested. Wilder heard it and felt the floor tilt. The two men had been carrying on a professional relationship entirely outside Odile's version of their lives. What else had been concealed?

The rented rooms had been closed long before the marriage ended. Wilder and Odile had split the crockery and surrendered the lease not because they were found out but because the afternoons had become a chore, the linen and plates another set of obligations. The parallel household they had built — those quiet rooms in a quiet district — had simply wound down, the way a clock does.

Before that, before the fatigue, there had been a dinner at the married couple's house where the two men discussed racquet games and schoolboy sport until Odile had no part in the talk at all. She sat at her own table and watched a friendship whose intimacy made her peripheral, a shared past she could not enter. Before the hotel there had been the pregnancy. Odile told Wilder she was carrying her husband's child, and the pair decided the rooms would go on exactly as before. The child would belong to the marriage. The afternoons would belong to them. It seemed, for a time, sustainable.

Wilder led Odile upstairs to a quiet room and told her how lovely she was. The affair began inside Emlyn's house, inside Emlyn's friendship, and neither of them understood yet how long the knowledge of it would sit in the room before anyone chose to name it.

He sinks to the bottom of the pool. The water presses against his ears and the tiled floor is cool and close and he does not struggle. His father's shadow moves across the surface above. He stays down there because staying down there is what his body knows how to do.

A man in a radio studio speaks about the fourth dimension. He tells the listeners that every moment exists at once, that death is merely attention fixed on a bad moment, that free will is an idea peculiar to this planet. The switchboard lights up. His daughter hears the broadcast and decides what she has already suspected: he is senile. She takes his accounts, his house, his practice, his days.

He is shot dead by a beam weapon after addressing a crowd. He has always known this would happen. He has always known the hour and the place. The lecture audience watches him fall. The assassin lowers the weapon. A promise made in a prison camp has been kept.

The prison camp sits beside a compound where enemy officers have been drawing double rations for years through a clerical error. The officers are plump and calm. The new arrivals are not. He is among the new arrivals, hollowed out, brought here on a train that smelled of gangrene and accusation. A scout on that train died with his last breath blaming him, and another prisoner on that train accepted the blame as an inheritance and promised that one day the debt would be collected.

He is born in a small industrial town. He grows into a weak, peculiar child. None of this surprises anyone.

He is held with other prisoners in a disused abattoir in a great city. The meat locker has a number on its door. Below ground, the air is cold and smells of old slaughter. Above ground, the city stands. Above ground, the city is destroyed by fire in one night. The prisoners come up in the morning and find it gone. They are made to dig bodies out of the cellars. One of the diggers dies of the dry heaves. The digging continues.

He comes home and collapses. In the hospital another patient hands him books by a hack science fiction writer. The books are full of flying saucers and time travel and improbable planets. He reads them all.

He marries the daughter of the man who owns the optometry school. He becomes rich. He fits people for glasses. He has a son who is a problem and a daughter who is a solution. His wife drives to the hospital after his plane crashes in the mountains. He survives the crash. She does not survive the drive. Exhaust fumes fill the car. She dies on the road while he lies in a bed that is not his own, breathing.

He is taken by aliens and kept in a zoo on their planet with a film actress. The enclosure is transparent. The aliens watch. The aliens explain that every moment exists at once. They explain that free will is an idea peculiar to his own planet. He understands this. He has always understood this. He has understood it since the bottom of the pool.

He is conscripted as a chaplain's assistant and shipped overseas with no training worth the name. He is lost behind the lines with a scout who beats him for wanting to be left to die. The winter fields are white and the scout's fists are hard and the walking does not stop. He wants to stop. He has always wanted to stop.

His daughter takes his affairs out of his hands. She believes she is protecting him. He does not resist. Resistance is not something his body knows how to do.

He goes on a radio talk show and tries to tell the world about the aliens and the fourth dimension. The world does not believe him. His daughter does not believe him. The lecture audience does not believe him either, but they listen, and listening is enough, and then the beam weapon fires and he falls and the moment he has always known arrives exactly as it has always existed.

He is on the bottom of the pool. He is in the meat locker. He is in the zoo. He is in the lecture hall. He is in the cold field with the scout's fist against his face. Every moment exists at once. He does not struggle. He has never struggled. The water is cool and close and he stays.
